title: JOINs
summary: A join combines related information from two tables by matching values.
introduction: A join combines related information from two tables by matching values. One list might hold book titles and another hold author names. Use the link between the lists to show both facts together.
learningObjectives: Join two or three tables on their key columns
Use table aliases to keep join queries readable
Keep unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN and find them with IS NULL
Recognise the missing ON condition and the LEFT JOIN that turns inner

blocks.text: Storing the customer's name in every order would duplicate it and let the copies drift apart when the name changes. Instead `orders.customer_id` points at `customers.id`. The price of that design is that a readable list of orders needs both tables, and `JOIN` is how you ask for it.

`JOIN ... ON` pairs each order with the customer whose id matches. Rows without a partner on either side are left out, which is why it is called an *inner* join (`INNER JOIN` and `JOIN` are synonyms). Table aliases (`orders AS o`) keep the column references short; the `AS` is optional.

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.quantity, o.ordered_on
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.content:
id | name              | quantity | ordered_on
---+-------------------+----------+-----------
1  | Ada Lovelace      | 1        | 2025-01-15
2  | Ada Lovelace      | 3        | 2025-01-15
3  | Grace Hopper      | 2        | 2025-02-02
4  | Linus Torvalds    | 1        | 2025-02-20
5  | Linus Torvalds    | 2        | 2025-03-11
6  | Margaret Hamilton | 10       | 2025-04-01
7  | Guido van Rossum  | 1        | 2025-04-18
8  | Grace Hopper      | 1        | 2025-05-05

blocks.text: Each additional table gets its own `JOIN ... ON`. Columns from any joined table can appear in the SELECT list and in expressions, such as the line total below. When two tables have a column with the same name (`name` exists in both customers and products) you must qualify it with the alias.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, o.quantity,
       p.price * o.quantity AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
ORDER BY o.id;

blocks.content:
customer          | product             | quantity | line_total
------------------+---------------------+----------+-----------
Ada Lovelace      | Mechanical keyboard | 1        | 89
Ada Lovelace      | Notebook            | 3        | 13.5
Grace Hopper      | USB cable           | 2        | 24
Linus Torvalds    | Monitor stand       | 1        | 39.5
Linus Torvalds    | Mouse pad           | 2        | 17.98
Margaret Hamilton | Sticky notes        | 10       | 27.5
Guido van Rossum  | Mechanical keyboard | 1        | 89
Grace Hopper      | Notebook            | 1        | 4.5

blocks.text: LEFT JOIN: keeping rows without a match

An inner join drops customers who have never ordered, which is exactly the wrong behaviour for a report of *all* customers. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL when there is no match. The example first adds a customer without orders so the effect is visible:

blocks.content:
OK: INSERT INTO customers (name, country, joined) VALUES ('Barbara Liskov', 'US', '2

name              | order_id
------------------+---------
Ada Lovelace      | 1
Ada Lovelace      | 2
Grace Hopper      | 3
Grace Hopper      | 8
Linus Torvalds    | 4
Linus Torvalds    | 5
Margaret Hamilton | 6
Guido van Rossum  | 7
Barbara Liskov    | NULL

blocks.text: Filtering on that NULL is the standard way to find rows *without* a match, here the customers who never ordered:

blocks.content:
OK: INSERT INTO customers (name, country, joined) VALUES ('Barbara Liskov', 'US', '2

name
--------------
Barbara Liskov

blocks.text: `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image (keep every row of the right table) and `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps both sides. SQLite supports them since version 3.39; MySQL has no FULL JOIN and emulates it with `UNION`. Most people write every outer join as a LEFT JOIN by putting the table to keep on the left.
A table can be joined with itself by giving it two aliases. This finds pairs of customers from the same country; `a.id < b.id` lists each pair once and avoids pairing a customer with themselves:

blocks.content:
customer     | compatriot
-------------+------------------
Grace Hopper | Margaret Hamilton

blocks.text: Omit the `ON` condition and the database pairs every row with every row, a *cross product*: 8 orders times 5 customers gives 40 rows. (`COUNT(*)` counts the rows; the next lesson explains it.)

blocks.title: A WHERE on the right table undoes a LEFT JOIN
blocks.text: `LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.quantity > 1` removes the NULL-filled rows again, because `NULL > 1` is not true, and silently turns the query into an inner join. Conditions on the optional table belong in the `ON` clause (`ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.quantity > 1`); only the `o.id IS NULL` test belongs in WHERE.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: List each product with the names of the customers who bought it, then insert a new product and change the join so that products nobody bought still appear.

blocks.title: Try it yourself
blocks.code:
SELECT p.name AS product, c.name AS customer, o.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY p.name;

questions.question: The customers table has 6 rows, one of them without orders, and there are 8 orders. How many rows does `SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id` return?
questions.explanation: Each order produces one row (8) and the customer without orders is kept with NULLs (1 more), so 9 rows. An inner join would return 8.

questions.question: `JOIN` and `INNER JOIN` mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: INNER is the default join type, so the keyword can be omitted. LEFT, RIGHT and FULL must be written out.

seo.title: SQL JOINs – INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and Self Joins
seo.description: Learn SQL JOINs: inner joins across two and three tables, LEFT JOIN with NULLs for missing matches, self joins, and two mistakes that change row counts.
